content: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are abnormal vascular connections that directly link the pulmonary artery to the pulmonary vein, bypassing the capillary system. This results in a right-to-left shunt, which can lead to significant clinical complications. These complications include paradoxical embolism, which may manifest as stroke or cerebral abscess, as well as pulmonary hemorrhage and hypoxemia. The presence of these malformations is associated with considerable morbidity and mortality. Embolisation is a minimally invasive endovascular procedure designed to treat PAVMs. The technique involves occluding the feeding arteries of the malformation, thereby eliminating the abnormal right-to-left shunting. This intervention aims to reduce the risk of complications associated with PAVMs, such as stroke and hypoxemia. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of embolisation in patients with PAVMs. This included comparisons with surgical resection and the use of different embolisation devices. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Trials Register, the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The last searches were performed in April and August 2017. References from review articles and cross-references were also examined. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in which patients with PAVMs were allocated to embolisation, no treatment, surgical resection, or embolisation using different devices. Two authors independently assessed studies for eligibility, with a third author reviewing excluded studies. However, no RCTs met the inclusion criteria, and no data analysis was performed. One ongoing trial was identified, which may be eligible for inclusion in the future. The main conclusion of the review is that there is currently no evidence from RCTs to support the use of embolisation for PAVMs. However, conducting RCTs in this context may not always be ethically feasible. Observational studies have provided accumulated data suggesting that embolisation is a safe procedure that reduces morbidity and mortality in patients with PAVMs. To strengthen the evidence base in the absence of RCTs, a standardized approach to reporting outcomes and long-term follow-up through registry studies is recommended.
